titulo: Belkhayate Timing Indicator: How to Use It in Practice
descricao: The Belkhayate Timing is a little-known oscillator that marks entry zones by color. See how to interpret each area and avoid the neutral middle zone.
corpo:
Not every technical analysis indicator goes mainstream, and the Belkhayate Timing is a good example of that. Created by trader Mustapha Belkhayate, it tries to calculate something like the center of gravity of price movement, helping identify both favorable entry zones and possible reversal points.

It's often described as a distant relative of the Stochastic and the RSI, since it also works on a bounded scale — from -10 to 10, or 0 to 100 depending on the platform — instead of tracking the price directly on the chart.

The indicator's three areas

Reading the Belkhayate Timing revolves around three visual regions, usually represented by different colors on the indicator panel:

  • Central area (neutral zone): when the indicator's value sits in this range, the traditional reading is that the odds of being right when entering the market are close to 50/50 — meaning there's no clear statistical edge to trade.
  • Red and green areas (extreme zones): the red area points to a possible price drop; the green one, to a possible rally. These are the regions that usually concentrate entries.
  • Upper and lower areas, beyond the extremes (warning zones): when the indicator goes past the red and green zones and enters these more distant ranges, the buy or sell signal is treated as higher probability.

How to interpret the numbers

On a -10 to 10 scale, values between -4 and -8 are usually read as a sell signal, and between 4 and 8 as a buy signal. The closer to 8 (or -8), or beyond that level, the stronger the signal is considered in the corresponding direction. Outside these ranges, in the middle of the scale, the indicator is essentially saying there's no clear edge to trade at that moment.

An example: if the indicator is showing 6.5 on a given candle, that would fall into the green zone/buy reading, but wouldn't yet have reached the stronger warning region (starting at 8). A value of -8.5, on the other hand, would be in the sell warning zone, indicating, according to the indicator's logic, a higher probability favoring a drop.

Why combine it with another indicator

The very concept behind the Belkhayate Timing suggests using it alongside channel indicators, like Bollinger Bands or the Belkhayate Barycenter itself (another indicator by the same author). The logic is similar to that of any extreme oscillator: a reversal signal becomes more consistent when the price is also touching a band or channel, not just when the oscillator alone reaches an extreme value.

Without this extra layer, the risk is the same as with any oscillator used in isolation: the indicator can stay stuck in an extreme zone for several candles in a row during a strong trend, and anyone selling just because the value passed 8 ends up exiting (or entering against the trend) at a moment still favorable to the ongoing move.

Where it tends to work best

Like most extreme oscillators, the Belkhayate Timing tends to do better in markets oscillating within a range, alternating between support and resistance, than in strong, prolonged trends. In a sideways market, touches on the red and green zones, especially combined with the price touching a Bollinger Band, tend to mark turning points more consistently.

An example of a combined reading

Imagine an asset trading within a R$ 45.00 to R$ 52.00 range for several weeks, without breaking either extreme. The price approaches R$ 51.50, touching the upper Bollinger Band, while the Belkhayate Timing rises to 7.8 — near the sell warning zone. The combination of the two signals, at the top of the trading range, forms a more consistent scenario for considering a sale than the indicator alone showing 7.8 in the middle of a chart with no defined range.

If the same value of 7.8 showed up during a strong uptrend, with the price breaking successive highs and no channel or sideways range to serve as reference, the same signal would lose much of its weight — the indicator could simply stay stuck in the warning zone for several candles in a row while the uptrend continues.

Using the indicator with caution

Being less widespread than the RSI or Stochastic, the Belkhayate Timing has less independent testing material available, which calls for even more caution before using it as the main basis of a strategy. It's worth treating it as one more layer of confirmation within a process that already includes trend context, support and resistance, and a defined stop plan — not as an isolated signal sufficient to open a position on its own. As with any extreme indicator, the risk of false signals exists, and no technical reading replaces consistent risk management.
